questions.title: NodePort

pic.say: Open the app on every node's port with a NodePort Service.

questions.words:
• NodePort Service = a Service that also opens one port on every node (30000 to 32767).
  • port / targetPort / nodePort = the Service's port / the container's port / the port on every node.
questions.think:
• Wanted: the pod declares port 80; a NodePort Service on 30080.
  • Look first: the container section of the Deployment.
  • Expect: no ports: under the container.
  • Fix: add the port, expose as NodePort, set the node port.
  • Prove: 80:30080/TCP, and a node answers on 30080.
questions.setup:
k delete namespace web --ignore-not-found
k create namespace web
k create deployment np --image=nginx:1.27 -n web
k rollout status deployment/np --timeout=120s -n web
clear
k get deployments,services -n web
questions.question:
In namespace `web`:
1. Edit deployment `np` so that the container declares port `80` (TCP).
2. Create a Service named `np-svc` of type `NodePort` that exposes the deployment on port `80`, using node port `30080`.
questions.meaning: Add a port to the Deployment, expose it, then fix the node port to 30080.

steps.title: Step 1. Add the container port
steps.html:
Why: containerPort tells Kubernetes which port the container listens on.

k edit deployment/np -n web

Type /image: and Enter. Add the last three lines, under name: nginx:

      containers:
      - image: nginx:1.27
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
        name: nginx
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP

Save with Esc, :wq. Then check the port:

k get deployment np -o jsonpath='{..ports}' -n web

Your prompt may follow on the same line.

You see:

deployment.apps/np edited
[{"containerPort":80,"protocol":"TCP"}]

Don't: start ports: under the - of - image:. It lines up with name:.

flow.h: Why: containerPort tells Kubernetes which port the container listens on.
Type /image: and Enter. Add the last three lines, under name: nginx:

flow.t:
containers:
      - image: nginx:1.27
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
        name: nginx
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          protocol: TCP

flow.h: Save with Esc, :wq. Then check the port:

flow.t: k get deployment np -o jsonpath='{..ports}' -n web

flow.h: Your prompt may follow on the same line.
You see:
Don't: start ports: under the - of - image:. It lines up with name:.

steps.title: Step 2. Expose it as NodePort
steps.html:
Why: k expose copies the Deployment's labels into the selector.

k expose deployment np --name=np-svc --port=80 --target-port=80 --type=NodePort -n web

You see:

service/np-svc exposed

Means: the Service exists, but with a random node port.

flow.h: Why: k expose copies the Deployment's labels into the selector.
You see:
Means: the Service exists, but with a random node port.

steps.title: Step 3. Set the node port
steps.html:
Why: there is no flag for it; patch the Service.

k patch service np-svc -p '{"spec":{"ports":[{"port":80,"nodePort":30080}]}}' -n web

You see:

service/np-svc patched

Means: the port with port: 80 now uses node port 30080.

flow.h: Why: there is no flag for it; patch the Service.
You see:
Means: the port with port: 80 now uses node port 30080.

steps.title: Step 4. Does the Service find the pod?
steps.html:
Why: no endpoints means no traffic, whatever the ports say.

k get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=np-svc -n web

ENDPOINTS must show a pod IP.

You see:

np-svc-...   IPv4   80   192.168.x.x   1m

Means: selector and target port are right.

flow.h: Why: no endpoints means no traffic, whatever the ports say.
ENDPOINTS must show a pod IP.
You see:
Means: selector and target port are right.

steps.title: Verify
steps.html:
Why: prove the node port answers.

k get service np-svc -n web
curl -s -m 3 node01:30080 | grep title

You see:

np-svc   NodePort   10.x.x.x   <none>   80:30080/TCP   2m
<title>Welcome to nginx!</title>

You see:

questions.title: Ingress

pic.say: Route web traffic by host name with an Ingress.

questions.words:
• Ingress = a rule for incoming web traffic: host + path → Service + port.
  • IngressClass = names the controller that carries out the rules.
  • pathType: Prefix = matches the path and everything below it. / matches every request.
questions.think:
• Wanted: host + path / → backend-svc:80.
  • Look first: the IngressClass name, and the Service port.
  • Expect: one class, nginx.
  • Fix: k create ingress with --class and --rule.
  • Prove: describe shows the backend with a pod IP.
questions.setup:
k delete namespace web --ignore-not-found
k create namespace web
k create deployment backend --image=nginx:1.27 -n web
k expose deployment backend --name=backend-svc --port=80 -n web
cat <<EOF | k apply -f -
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: IngressClass
metadata:
  name: nginx
spec:
  controller: k8s.io/ingress-nginx
EOF
k rollout status deployment/backend --timeout=120s -n web
clear
k get ingressclass,services,ingress -n web
questions.question: In namespace `web`, create an Ingress named `web-ing` that uses the existing IngressClass. Requests for host `shop.example.com` with path `/` (type Prefix) must go to service `backend-svc` on port `80`.
questions.meaning: One Ingress, made with one command. Only the class name must be looked up.

steps.title: Step 1. Which class exists?
steps.html:
Why: an Ingress without the right class is ignored.

k get ingressclass

You see:

nginx   k8s.io/ingress-nginx   <none>   1m

Means: the class is nginx.

flow.h: Why: an Ingress without the right class is ignored.

steps.html:
Why: the rule needs the Service port, not the pod port.

k get service backend-svc -n web

You see:

backend-svc   ClusterIP   10.x.x.x   <none>   80/TCP   1m

Means: backend-svc:80 is a real target.

Means: backend-svc:80 is a real target.

steps.title: Step 3. Create the Ingress
steps.html:
Why: k create ingress writes the whole object; no YAML.

k create ingress web-ing --class=nginx --rule="shop.example.com/*=backend-svc:80" -n web

You see:

ingress.networking.k8s.io/web-ing created

Means: rule = HOST/PATH=SERVICE:PORT. The * makes the path type Prefix.
Don't: drop the *. Without it the path type is Exact.

questions.title: Gateway API (replace an Ingress)

pic.say: Replace an Ingress with a Gateway and an HTTPRoute.

questions.words:
• Gateway = the entry point: port, protocol, hostname, TLS. It names a GatewayClass (the controller).
  • HTTPRoute = which host and path go to which Service and port.
questions.think:
• Wanted: Gateway (host + TLS) and HTTPRoute (path → Service).
  • Look first: the Ingress, and the GatewayClass name.
  • Expect: host, TLS secret, path, Service, port.
  • Fix: docs examples, with those values filled in.
  • Prove: both objects exist, the route is attached, the Ingress is gone.
questions.setup:
k get crd gateways.gateway.networking.k8s.io >/dev/null 2>&1 || k apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.2.1/standard-install.yaml
k wait --for=condition=Established crd/gateways.gateway.networking.k8s.io crd/httproutes.gateway.networking.k8s.io --timeout=60s
k delete namespace web --ignore-not-found
rm -f gw.yaml route.yaml
k create namespace web
k create deployment backend --image=nginx:1.27 -n web
k expose deployment backend --name=backend-svc --port=80 -n web
openssl req -x509 -nodes -newkey rsa:2048 -days 30 -subj "/CN=shop.example.com" -keyout /tmp/t.key -out /tmp/t.crt 2>/dev/null
k create secret tls web-tls --cert=/tmp/t.crt --key=/tmp/t.key -n web
cat <<EOF | k apply -f -
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata:
  name: nginx
spec:
  controllerName: gateway.nginx.org/nginx-gateway-controller
EOF
k create ingress web-ing --class=nginx --rule="shop.example.com/*=backend-svc:80,tls=web-tls" -n web
k rollout status deployment/backend --timeout=120s -n web
clear
k get ingress,gatewayclass -n web

questions.title: NetworkPolicy: allow one app to reach another

pic.say: Allow only one app to reach another.

questions.words:
• podSelector (top) = the pods this policy protects. Under from:: the pods allowed in.
  • AND / OR in from = two selectors under ONE - must both match. Each new - is another allowed source.
  • CNI enforcement = the network plugin applies policies. Without support, they are silently ignored.
questions.think:
• Wanted: only api reaches db on port 80.
  • Look first: the real pod labels.
  • Expect: app=db, app=api, app=other.
  • Fix: one policy: protect db, allow api, port 80.
  • Prove: api gets the page, other times out.
questions.setup:

rm -f np.yaml
k create namespace prod
k run db --image=nginx:1.27 --labels=app=db -n prod
k run api --image=busybox:1.36 --labels=app=api -n prod -- sleep 3600

k expose pod db --name=db-svc --port=80 -n prod

steps.title: Step 2. Write the policy
steps.html:
Why: there is no k create networkpolicy. Copy the example from the docs page "Network Policies", section "The NetworkPolicy resource".

vim np.yaml

The finished file. Yours: name, namespace, the two app: labels and the port:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: db-policy
  namespace: prod
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: db
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: api
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80

Means: from the docs copy, delete - Egress, the ipBlock and namespaceSelector items, and the whole egress: part.
Don't: keep - Egress. With no egress rules, db can send nothing out.

questions.title: Default deny, but keep DNS

pic.say: Block everything but keep DNS working.

questions.words:
• Egress = traffic going OUT of the selected pods.
  • Default deny = a policy with podSelector: {}. It selects all pods and allows nothing.
  • Port 53 = the DNS port, on UDP and TCP.
questions.think:
• Wanted: every pod in prod cut off, except DNS going out.
  • Look first: traffic flows now, and no policy exists yet.
  • Expect: No resources found, and wget gets the nginx page.
  • Fix: the docs "default deny all" policy plus an egress rule for port 53.
  • Prove: a name lookup works, a download times out.
questions.setup:
k delete namespace prod --ignore-not-found
rm -f deny.yaml
k create namespace prod
k run app --image=busybox:1.36 -n prod -- sleep 3600
k run web --image=nginx:1.27 --port=80 --expose -n prod
k wait --for=condition=Ready pod/app pod/web --timeout=120s -n prod
clear

questions.question: In namespace `prod`, create a NetworkPolicy named `default-deny` that blocks all incoming and all outgoing traffic for every pod in the namespace. DNS lookups (port 53, UDP and TCP) must still work.
questions.meaning: One policy for all pods: nothing in, only port 53 out.

steps.title: Step 2. Write the policy
steps.html:
Why: there is no k create networkpolicy. Copy from the docs page "Network Policies", section "Default policies", box "Default deny all ingress and all egress traffic".

vim deny.yaml

The finished file. Yours: name, namespace and the whole egress: part:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny
  namespace: prod
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  - Egress
  egress:
  - ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53

Means: no ingress: part, so nothing comes in. Out, only port 53.
Don't: add to: under egress. Without to:, port 53 is open to any DNS server.

questions.title: TLS settings in a ConfigMap

pic.say: Change a setting inside a ConfigMap and restart the app.

questions.words:
• ssl_protocols = the nginx line that lists the TLS versions it accepts.
  • openssl s_client = opens a TLS connection. -tls1_2 forces version 1.2.
questions.think:
• Wanted: nginx accepts only TLSv1.3.
  • Look first: the ssl_protocols line in the ConfigMap.
  • Expect: ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;
  • Fix: remove TLSv1.2, then restart the Deployment.
  • Prove: a TLSv1.2 handshake fails, a TLSv1.3 handshake works.
questions.setup:
k delete namespace nginx-static --ignore-not-found
rm -f /root/cm-backup.yaml
k create namespace nginx-static
openssl req -x509 -nodes -newkey rsa:2048 -days 30 -subj "/CN=nginx-static" -keyout /tmp/tls.key -out /tmp/tls.crt 2>/dev/null
k create secret tls nginx-tls --cert=/tmp/tls.crt --key=/tmp/tls.key -n nginx-static
cat <<'EOF' > /tmp/nginx.conf
events {}
http {
  server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/tls/tls.crt;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/tls/tls.key;
    ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;
    location / { return 200 "hello\n"; }
  }
}
EOF
k create configmap nginx-config --from-file=nginx.conf=/tmp/nginx.conf -n nginx-static
cat <<EOF | k apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx-static
  namespace: nginx-static
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx-static
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx-static
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.27
        ports:
        - containerPort: 443
        volumeMounts:
        - name: config
          mountPath: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
          subPath: nginx.conf
        - name: tls
          mountPath: /etc/nginx/tls
      volumes:
      - name: config
        configMap:
          name: nginx-config
      - name: tls
        secret:
          secretName: nginx-tls
EOF
k expose deployment nginx-static --port=443 -n nginx-static
k rollout status deployment/nginx-static --timeout=120s -n nginx-static
clear
k get configmap nginx-config -o yaml -n nginx-static | grep ssl_protocols
questions.question: In namespace `nginx-static`, deployment `nginx-static` gets its configuration from ConfigMap `nginx-config`. The server currently accepts TLSv1.2 and TLSv1.3. Change the configuration so that ONLY TLSv1.3 is accepted, and make sure the running pods use the new configuration.
questions.meaning: Delete TLSv1.2 from one line of the ConfigMap, then restart the pods.

steps.title: Step 1. Back up the ConfigMap
steps.html:
Why: one wrong character breaks nginx. A backup lets you start over.

k get configmap nginx-config -o yaml -n nginx-static > /root/cm-backup.yaml
grep ssl_protocols /root/cm-backup.yaml

This is the line to change: TLSv1.2 must go.

You see:

    ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;

Means: the backup holds the old line. Now change the real one.

flow.h: Why: one wrong character breaks nginx. A backup lets you start over.

flow.t: k get configmap nginx-config -o yaml -n nginx-static > /root/cm-backup.yaml

flow.h: This is the line to change: TLSv1.2 must go.
You see:
Means: the backup holds the old line. Now change the real one.

steps.title: Step 2. How do the pods get the file?
steps.html:
Why: the mount decides whether the pods ever see a change.

k get deployment nginx-static -o yaml -n nginx-static | grep subPath

You see:

          subPath: nginx.conf

Means: a subPath file never updates. The pods need a restart.

flow.h: Why: the mount decides whether the pods ever see a change.

flow.t: k get deployment nginx-static -o yaml -n nginx-static | grep subPath

flow.h: You see:
Means: a subPath file never updates. The pods need a restart.

steps.title: Step 3. Remove TLSv1.2
steps.html:
Why: the setting lives inside the ConfigMap's nginx.conf text.

k edit configmap/nginx-config -n nginx-static

In vim: type /ssl_protocols, Enter. Then type :s/TLSv1.2 //, Enter. Save with :wq. Then check the line:

k get configmap nginx-config -o yaml -n nginx-static | grep ssl_protocols

You see:

configmap/nginx-config edited
    ssl_protocols TLSv1.3;

Means: only TLSv1.3 is left, and the ; is still there.
Don't: delete the ; at the end. nginx then fails to start.

flow.h: Why: the setting lives inside the ConfigMap's nginx.conf text.

steps.title: Step 4. Restart the pods
steps.html:
Why: nginx reads its config only when it starts.

k rollout restart deployment/nginx-static -n nginx-static
k rollout status deployment/nginx-static -n nginx-static

The restart makes a new pod, and the new pod reads the new config.

You see:

deployment.apps/nginx-static restarted
deployment "nginx-static" successfully rolled out

flow.h: Why: nginx reads its config only when it starts.
The restart makes a new pod, and the new pod reads the new config.

flow.t:

steps.title: Verify
steps.html:
Why: prove the server refuses TLSv1.2 and accepts TLSv1.3.

IP=$(k get service nginx-static -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}' -n nginx-static)
openssl s_client -connect $IP:443 -tls1_2 </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E 'alert|New,'
openssl s_client -connect $IP:443 -tls1_3 </dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E 'alert|New,'

alert protocol version = TLSv1.2 refused. New, TLSv1.3 = TLSv1.3 works.

You see:

...:tlsv1 alert protocol version:...
New, (NONE), Cipher is (NONE)
New, TLSv1.3, Cipher is ...

Don't: test before Step 4. The old pod still accepts TLSv1.2.

questions.title: CoreDNS config

pic.say: Change CoreDNS's configuration.

questions.words:
• Corefile = the CoreDNS config text, in ConfigMap coredns, namespace kube-system.
  • .:53 { } = the main block of the Corefile. Each line inside is a plugin.
  • rewrite name A B = a question for name A is answered as if it asked for B.
questions.think:
• Wanted: api.example.com answers with the IP of backend-svc.
  • Look first: the Service's CLUSTER-IP, then the Corefile.
  • Expect: no rewrite line in the Corefile yet.
  • Fix: backup, add rewrite name A B, restart CoreDNS.
  • Prove: a test pod resolves api.example.com to the CLUSTER-IP.
questions.setup:
k delete namespace web --ignore-not-found
k delete pod t --ignore-not-found
[ -f /root/coredns-backup.yaml ] && k replace --force -f /root/coredns-backup.yaml
k get configmap coredns -o yaml -n kube-system | sed '/rewrite name api.example.com/d' | k replace -f -
rm -f /root/coredns-backup.yaml
k scale deployment/coredns --replicas=2 -n kube-system
k rollout restart deployment/coredns -n kube-system
k rollout status deployment/coredns --timeout=120s -n kube-system
k create namespace web
k create deployment backend --image=nginx:1.27 -n web
k expose deployment backend --name=backend-svc --port=80 -n web
k rollout status deployment/backend --timeout=120s -n web
clear
k get configmap coredns -o jsonpath='{.data.Corefile}' -n kube-system
questions.question: Configure cluster DNS so that the name `api.example.com` resolves to the service `backend-svc` in namespace `web`, for all pods in the cluster. Make sure CoreDNS uses the new configuration.
questions.meaning: Add one rewrite line to the Corefile, then restart CoreDNS.

steps.title: Step 1. Back up the Corefile
steps.html:
Why: one typo breaks DNS for the whole cluster. The backup is your way back.

k get configmap coredns -o yaml -n kube-system > /root/coredns-backup.yaml
ls /root/coredns-backup.yaml

You see:

/root/coredns-backup.yaml

Means: you can always restore the original.

flow.h: Why: one typo breaks DNS for the whole cluster. The backup is your way back.

flow.t: k get configmap coredns -o yaml -n kube-system > /root/coredns-backup.yaml

flow.h: You see:
Means: you can always restore the original.

steps.title: Step 2. Which IP should the name give?
steps.html:
Why: you need it to judge the test at the end.

k get service backend-svc -n web

Note the CLUSTER-IP.

You see:

backend-svc   ClusterIP   10.x.x.x   <none>   80/TCP   1m

Means: the full target name is backend-svc.web.svc.cluster.local.

flow.h: Why: you need it to judge the test at the end.
Note the CLUSTER-IP.
You see:
Means: the full target name is backend-svc.web.svc.cluster.local.

steps.title: Step 3. Add the rewrite line
steps.html:
Why: the Corefile lives in ConfigMap coredns. The docs page "Customizing DNS Service" shows it.

k edit configmap/coredns -n kube-system

Put the cursor on ready. Press o. Add the rewrite line with that same indent:

  Corefile: |
    .:53 {
        errors
        health {
           lameduck 5s
        }
        ready
        rewrite name api.example.com backend-svc.web.svc.cluster.local
        kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {

Save with Esc, :wq.

You see:

configmap/coredns edited

Don't: put the line outside .:53 { }. CoreDNS then ignores it or crashes.

flow.h: Why: the Corefile lives in ConfigMap coredns. The docs page "Customizing DNS Service" shows it.

steps.html:
Why: new pods load the new Corefile at once.

...

coredns-...   1/1   Running   0   15s
coredns-...   1/1   Running   0   20s

Means: CoreDNS runs with your line.

coredns-...   1/1   Running   0   20s

flow.h: Means: CoreDNS runs with your line.

steps.html:

You see:

...
Address: 10.x.x.x  <-- Step 2

questions.title: Sidecar container

pic.say: Add a helper container next to the main one.

questions.words:
• Sidecar = a helper container in the same pod.
  • emptyDir = an empty folder owned by the pod, shared by its mounts.
  • volumeMounts = where a volume appears inside one container.
questions.think:
• Wanted: a second container reading the main one's log.
  • Look first: the Deployment's YAML, saved to a file.
  • Expect: one container, named busybox, no volumes.
  • Fix: volume, mount in main, sidecar with the same mount.
  • Prove: READY 2/2; the sidecar logs dates.
questions.setup:
k delete namespace work --ignore-not-found
rm -f app.yaml app-backup.yaml
k create namespace work
k create deployment app --image=busybox:1.36 -n work -- sh -c "while true; do date >> /var/log/app.log; sleep 2; done"
k rollout status deployment/app --timeout=120s -n work
clear
k get pods -n work
questions.question: In namespace `work`, deployment `app` writes its log to `/var/log/app.log`. Add a sidecar container named `log-shipper` with image `busybox:1.36` that runs `tail -f /var/log/app.log`. Use a shared volume named `logs` mounted at `/var/log` in both containers. Do not change the existing container's image or command.
questions.meaning: One volume, mounted in the old container and in a new one.

questions.title: HPA (autoscaling)

pic.say: Scale pods automatically with CPU load.

questions.words:
• HPA = HorizontalPodAutoscaler. Sets the replica count by CPU use.
  • metrics-server = the add-on that measures pod CPU.
  • Stabilization window = how long the HPA waits before it removes pods.
questions.think:
• Wanted: an HPA: min, max, CPU target, scale-down window.
  • Look first: does the Deployment have a CPU request?
  • Expect: cpu: 100m under requests.
  • Fix: k autoscale, then add behavior with k edit.
  • Prove: TARGETS shows a number; the window reads 30.
questions.setup:
k delete namespace shop --ignore-not-found
k create namespace shop
k create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27 -n shop
k set resources deployment/web --requests=cpu=100m -n shop
k apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server/releases/download/v0.8.0/components.yaml
k get deployment metrics-server -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].args}' -n kube-system | grep -q kubelet-insecure-tls || k patch deployment metrics-server --type=json -p='[{"op":"add","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/args/-","value":"--kubelet-insecure-tls"}]' -n kube-system
k rollout status deployment/metrics-server --timeout=180s -n kube-system
k rollout status deployment/web --timeout=120s -n shop
for i in $(seq 1 24); do k top node >/dev/null 2>&1 && break; sleep 5; done
clear
k get hpa -n shop

questions.title: Share a node's resources between pods

pic.say: Split a node's CPU and memory fairly between pods.

questions.words:
• Allocatable = the CPU and memory a node offers to pods in total.
  • Allocated resources = what running pods already requested.
  • Request = what one pod reserves.
questions.think:
• Wanted: three equal requests, 10% left free.
  • Look first: the node's Allocatable and Allocated resources.
  • Expect: other pods already reserve some.
  • Fix: free × 0.9 ÷ 3, rounded down.
  • Prove: 3 pods Running; node near 90%.
questions.setup:
k delete namespace shop --ignore-not-found
k create namespace shop
cat <<EOF | k apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  namespace: shop
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        kubernetes.io/hostname: node01
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.27
EOF
k rollout status deployment/web --timeout=120s -n shop
clear
k get pods -o wide -n shop
questions.question: In namespace `shop`, deployment `web` runs `3` replicas, all on node `node01`. Set CPU and memory requests so that the three pods share the node's available resources equally. Leave roughly 10% headroom so the node stays stable. All 3 pods must be Running afterwards.
questions.meaning: Request per pod = free resources × 0.9 ÷ 3, for CPU and for memory.

steps.title: Step 1. Take `web` out of the numbers
steps.html:
Why: then the node shows only OTHER pods' requests.

k scale deployment/web --replicas=0 -n shop

You see:

deployment.apps/web scaled

flow.h: Why: then the node shows only OTHER pods' requests.
You see:

steps.title: Step 2. Read the node's two numbers
steps.html:
Why: free = offered minus reserved.

k describe node node01 | grep -A7 "Allocatable:"
k describe node node01 | grep -A6 "Allocated resources:"

Read cpu and memory twice: under Allocatable (offered) and in the Requests column (reserved). This is an example; your numbers differ.

You see:

Allocatable:
  cpu:                1
  ...
  memory:             1843756Ki
...
  Resource           Requests     Limits
  --------           --------     ------
  cpu                250m (25%)   0 (0%)
  memory             200Mi (11%)  0 (0%)

Means: CPU 1000m − 250m. Memory 1843756Ki − 200Mi.
Don't: take the Limits column. Use Requests.

flow.h: Why: free = offered minus reserved.

flow.t: k describe node node01 | grep -A6 "Allocated resources:"

flow.h: Read cpu and memory twice: under Allocatable (offered) and in the Requests column (reserved). This is an example; your numbers differ.
You see:

flow.t:
Allocatable:
  cpu:                1
  ...
  memory:             1843756Ki
...
  Resource           Requests     Limits
  --------           --------     ------
  cpu                250m (25%)   0 (0%)
  memory             200Mi (11%)  0 (0%)

flow.h: Means: CPU 1000m − 250m. Memory 1843756Ki − 200Mi. Don't: take the Limits column. Use Requests.

steps.title: Step 3. Calculate
steps.html:
Why: the shell does the maths. $(( )) always rounds down.

echo $(( 1843756 / 1024 ))
echo $(( (1000 - 250) * 9 / 10 / 3 ))
echo $(( (1800 - 200) * 9 / 10 / 3 ))

You see:

1800  <-- memory Mi
225   <-- CPU/pod (m)
480   <-- mem/pod (Mi)

Means: CPU 750m × 0.9 ÷ 3 = 225m. Memory 1600Mi × 0.9 ÷ 3 = 480Mi.
Don't: copy these numbers. Use your own from Step 2.

flow.h: Why: the shell does the maths. $(( )) always rounds down.
You see:
Means: CPU 750m × 0.9 ÷ 3 = 225m. Memory 1600Mi × 0.9 ÷ 3 = 480Mi. Don't: copy these numbers. Use your own from Step 2.

steps.title: Step 4. Set the requests, bring the pods back
steps.html:
Why: the requests apply to every new pod.

k set resources deployment/web --requests=cpu=225m,memory=480Mi -n shop
k scale deployment/web --replicas=3 -n shop

You see:

deployment.apps/web resource requirements updated
deployment.apps/web scaled

flow.h: Why: the requests apply to every new pod.
You see:

flow.t:
deployment.apps/web resource requirements updated
deployment.apps/web scaled

steps.title: Verify
steps.html:
Why: prove all 3 fit, near 90%.

k get pods -o wide -n shop
k describe node node01 | grep -A6 "Allocated resources:"

Three pod lines like the first one, all on node01.

You see:

web-...   1/1   Running   0   20s   ...   node01
...
  cpu                925m (92%)    0 (0%)
  memory             1640Mi (91%)  0 (0%)

flow.h: Why: prove all 3 fit, near 90%.

flow.t: k describe node node01 | grep -A6 "Allocated resources:"

flow.h: Three pod lines like the first one, all on node01.
You see:

questions.wrong:
You see Cause Fix
one pod Pending, Events: Insufficient cpu (or memory) requests slightly too big lower them 10%, repeat Step 4

story.broken: Three web dishes fight over node01's space; some can't get a seat.
story.fix: Scale to 0, split free CPU/memory (keep ~10% spare) by 3, set requests, scale back to 3.

coach.pattern: Compute requests from node allocatable, split across replicas

clues.q: share the node's available resources equally

clues.means: Multiply the free amount by 0.9, round down

clues.q: All 3 pods must be Running afterwards
clues.means: Scale to 0 first, set requests, scale back to 3 and check

traps.do: Use `Allocatable:`, because that is what pods may use after the system's own reserve

traps.dont: Calculating while web's 3 pods still hold requests
traps.do: `k scale deployment/web --replicas=0 -n shop` first, because web's old requests would count as used
`k set resources deployment/web --requests=cpu=<X>m,memory=<Y>Mi -n shop`, because the task asks for requests

verify.cmd: k describe node node01 | grep -A6 "Allocated resources:"

memorise: k describe node node01 | grep -A6 "Allocated resources:"
k scale deployment/web --replicas=3 -n shop; k get pods -o wide -n shop
coach.plan: Equal requests, 10% headroom → scale to 0 → describe node (Allocatable − Requests) → free × 0.9 ÷ 3 → set resources --requests, scale to 3 → 3 Running, node ~90%

kw.hint: Replicas → scale the deployment
kw.cmds: k scale deployment/<name> --replicas=<n> -n <ns>

kw.hint: Requests/limits → set resources on the deployment, then check the pods schedule
kw.cmds:
k set resources deployment/<name> --requests=cpu=<c>,memory=<m> --limits=cpu=<c>,memory=<m> -n <ns>
k describe node <node> | grep -A6 Allocated

questions.title: ConfigMap and Secret in a pod

pic.say: Feed settings and passwords into a pod.

questions.words:
• ConfigMap = plain settings stored as KEY=VALUE.
  • Secret = the same, for sensitive values like passwords.
  • envFrom = turns every key of a ConfigMap into an environment variable.
  • volumes + volumeMounts = volumes names the storage; volumeMounts shows it at a path. Each key becomes a file.
questions.think:
• Wanted: a ConfigMap, a Secret, and a pod that uses both.
  • Look first: what already exists in app.
  • Expect: only kube-root-ca.crt (every namespace has it).
  • Fix: create both imperatively; pod YAML from dry-run plus two blocks.
  • Prove: the variable and the file exist inside the pod.
questions.setup:
k delete namespace app --ignore-not-found
rm -f pod.yaml
k create namespace app
clear
k get configmaps,secrets -n app
questions.question:
In namespace `app`:
1. Create a ConfigMap named `app-cfg` with the key `LOG_LEVEL` and value `debug`.
2. Create a Secret named `db-sec` with the key `password` and value `s3cret`.
3. Create a pod named `api` with image `nginx:1.27`. All keys of the ConfigMap must be available as environment variables. The Secret must be mounted as files under `/etc/db`.
questions.meaning: Two one-line creates, then a pod YAML with envFrom and a Secret volume.

steps.title: Step 1. Create the ConfigMap and the Secret
steps.html:
Why: both have a one-line create command. No YAML needed.

k create configmap app-cfg --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=debug -n app
k create secret generic db-sec --from-literal=password=s3cret -n app

You see:

configmap/app-cfg created
secret/db-sec created

Don't: forget generic. k create secret alone needs a type.

flow.h: Why: both have a one-line create command. No YAML needed.

flow.t: k create secret generic db-sec --from-literal=password=s3cret -n app

flow.h: You see:
Don't: forget generic. k create secret alone needs a type.

steps.title: Step 2. Generate the pod YAML
steps.html:
Why: --dry-run=client -o yaml prints the YAML and creates nothing.

k run api --image=nginx:1.27 --dry-run=client -o yaml -n app > pod.yaml
cat pod.yaml

resources: shows the container level (4 spaces in). dnsPolicy: shows the pod level (2 spaces in).

You see:

...
spec:
  containers:
  - image: nginx:1.27
    name: api
    resources: {}
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
...

flow.h: Why: --dry-run=client -o yaml prints the YAML and creates nothing.

flow.t: k run api --image=nginx:1.27 --dry-run=client -o yaml -n app > pod.yaml

flow.h: resources: shows the container level (4 spaces in). dnsPolicy: shows the pod level (2 spaces in).
You see:

flow.t:
...
spec:
  containers:
  - image: nginx:1.27
    name: api
    resources: {}
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
...

steps.title: Step 3. Add envFrom and the Secret volume
steps.html:
Why: copy the blocks from the docs pages "Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap" and "Secrets".

vim pod.yaml

The finished file. New: the envFrom:, volumeMounts: and volumes: blocks:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  labels:
    run: api
  name: api
  namespace: app
spec:
  containers:
  - image: nginx:1.27
    name: api
    resources: {}
    envFrom:
    - configMapRef:
        name: app-cfg
    volumeMounts:
    - name: db
      mountPath: /etc/db
  volumes:
  - name: db
    secret:
      secretName: db-sec
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
  restartPolicy: Always

Means: envFrom and volumeMounts sit at container level. volumes sits at pod level. The name db links them.
Don't: delete other lines your file has, like status: {}. They do no harm.

Vim tip: type :set paste before you press i and paste. Save with :wq.

flow.h: Why: copy the blocks from the docs pages "Configure a Pod to Use a ConfigMap" and "Secrets".
The finished file. New: the envFrom:, volumeMounts: and volumes: blocks:

flow.t:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  labels:
    run: api
  name: api

    - configMapRef:
        name: app-cfg
    volumeMounts:
    - name: db
      mountPath: /etc/db
  volumes:
  - name: db
    secret:
      secretName: db-sec
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
  restartPolicy: Always

flow.h: Means: envFrom and volumeMounts sit at container level. volumes sits at pod level. The name db links them. Don't: delete other lines your file has, like status: {}. They do no harm.
Vim tip: type :set paste before you press i and paste. Save with :wq.

steps.title: Step 4. Create the pod
steps.html:
Why: the file does nothing until the cluster has it.

k apply -f pod.yaml
k get pod api -n app

You see:

pod/api created
api   1/1   Running   0   10s

flow.h: Why: the file does nothing until the cluster has it.
You see:

steps.title: Verify
steps.html:
Why: prove the variable and the file are inside the container.

k exec api -n app -- env | grep LOG_LEVEL
k exec api -n app -- cat /etc/db/password

The file has no newline at the end, so your prompt may follow s3cret on the same line.

You see:

LOG_LEVEL=debug
s3cret

flow.h: Why: prove the variable and the file are inside the container.

flow.t: k exec api -n app -- env | grep LOG_LEVEL

flow.h: The file has no newline at the end, so your prompt may follow s3cret on the same line.
You see:

questions.wrong:
You see Cause Fix
STATUS CreateContainerConfigError the ConfigMap name in envFrom does not exist k describe pod api -n app names it; delete the pod, fix, apply again
STATUS stays ContainerCreating the Secret name in volumes does not exist read Events in k describe pod api -n app; fix secretName:
unknown field "spec.containers[0].volumes" volumes: is indented under the container move it to the column of containers:
Forbidden: pod updates may not change fields other than ... a pod's env and volumes cannot change k delete pod api -n app, then apply again

story.broken: Dish api needs its recipe card (ConfigMap) and secret sauce (Secret), but neither exists.
story.fix: Create cm app-cfg and secret db-sec, then give them to pod api as env vars.

coach.pattern: ConfigMap as env (envFrom) + Secret as volume in a pod

clues.q: All keys of the ConfigMap must be available as environment variables
The Secret must be mounted as files under `/etc/db`

traps.do: `envFrom: - configMapRef: name: app-cfg`, because envFrom loads all keys of the ConfigMap at once
`secret: secretName: db-sec`, because secret volumes use `secretName`, not `name`
Add `-n app` to the cm, secret and pod, because a pod can only use ConfigMaps and Secrets from its own namespace

memorise: k create secret generic db-sec --from-literal=password=s3cret -n app
k run api --image=nginx:1.27 --dry-run=client -o yaml -n app > pod.yaml

questions.cmds:
k create configmap app-cfg --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=debug -n app
k create secret generic db-sec --from-literal=password=s3cret -n app
k run api --image=nginx:1.27 --dry-run=client -o yaml -n app > pod.yaml
cat pod.yaml
vim pod.yaml
# file content:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  labels:
    run: api
  name: api
  namespace: app
spec:
  containers:
  - image: nginx:1.27
    name: api
    resources: {}
    envFrom:
    - configMapRef:
        name: app-cfg
    volumeMounts:
    - name: db
      mountPath: /etc/db
  volumes:
  - name: db
    secret:
      secretName: db-sec
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
  restartPolicy: Always
k apply -f pod.yaml
k get pod api -n app
k exec api -n app -- env | grep LOG_LEVEL
k exec api -n app -- cat /etc/db/password

kw.hint: ConfigMap → create from literal/file, mount or envFrom, restart pods to pick it up
kw.cmds:
k create configmap <name> --from-literal=<k>=<v> -n <ns>
k edit configmap/<name> -n <ns>
k rollout restart deployment/<name> -n <ns>

kw.hint: Secret → generic or tls; check with describe (values stay hidden)
kw.cmds:
k create secret generic <name> --from-literal=<k>=<v> -n <ns>
k create secret tls <name> --cert=<crt> --key=<key> -n <ns>
k describe secret <name> -n <ns>

kw.hint: Output to a file → redirect exactly to the path in the question; check with cat
kw.cmds:
k logs <pod> -n <ns> > /opt/<file>
cat /opt/<file>

questions.title: Taint, toleration, nodeSelector

pic.say: Send a pod to one node, and let it past that node's taint.

questions.words:
• Taint = a mark on a node, key=value:effect. NoSchedule: no new pods, unless they tolerate it.
  • nodeSelector = pod lines: "only put me on a node with this label".
questions.think:
• Wanted: pod x running on the tainted node01.
  • Look first: the taints on node01.
  • Expect: <none> before you start.
  • Fix: toleration (allowed there) + nodeSelector (sent there).
  • Prove: the pod's NODE column says node01.
questions.setup:
k delete pod x --ignore-not-found
rm -f x.yaml
k taint nodes node01 env=prod:NoSchedule- || true
k label nodes node01 env-
clear
k describe node node01 | grep -i taints
questions.question:
1. Taint node `node01` with `env=prod:NoSchedule`.
2. Label node `node01` with `env=prod`.
3. Create a pod named `x` with image `nginx:1.27` in namespace `default` that tolerates the taint and is scheduled on `node01`.
questions.meaning: Mark the node twice, then a pod YAML with a toleration and a nodeSelector.

steps.title: Step 1. Taint and label the node
steps.html:
Why: the taint keeps pods away; the label lets a pod pick this node.

k taint nodes node01 env=prod:NoSchedule
k label nodes node01 env=prod

You see:

node/node01 tainted
node/node01 labeled

flow.h: Why: the taint keeps pods away; the label lets a pod pick this node.
You see:

steps.title: Step 2. Check both marks
steps.html:
Why: a typo here breaks the pod later.

k describe node node01 | grep -i taints
k get node node01 -L env

You see:

Taints:             env=prod:NoSchedule   <-- taint
NAME     STATUS   ROLES    AGE   VERSION   ENV
node01   Ready    <none>   ...   v1.35.x   prod   <-- label

Means: the node is ready for the pod.

flow.h: Why: a typo here breaks the pod later.

flow.t: k describe node node01 | grep -i taints

flow.h: You see:

flow.t:
Taints:             env=prod:NoSchedule   <-- taint
NAME     STATUS   ROLES    AGE   VERSION   ENV
node01   Ready    <none>   ...   v1.35.x   prod   <-- label

flow.h: Means: the node is ready for the pod.

steps.title: Step 3. Generate the pod YAML
steps.html:
Why: --dry-run=client -o yaml prints the YAML and creates nothing.

k run x --image=nginx:1.27 --dry-run=client -o yaml > x.yaml
grep -n containers x.yaml

The new blocks go above containers:, in the same column.

You see:

...  containers:

flow.h: Why: --dry-run=client -o yaml prints the YAML and creates nothing.
The new blocks go above containers:, in the same column.
You see:

steps.title: Step 4. Add the toleration and the nodeSelector
steps.html:
Why: copy from the docs pages "Taints and Tolerations" and "Assign Pods to Nodes".

vim x.yaml

The finished file. New: the nodeSelector: and tolerations: blocks:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  labels:
    run: x
  name: x
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    env: prod
  tolerations:
  - key: "env"
    operator: "Equal"
    value: "prod"
    effect: "NoSchedule"
  containers:
  - image: nginx:1.27
    name: x
    resources: {}
  dnsPolicy: ClusterFirst
  restartPolicy: Always

Means: the docs say key1 and value1. Use the taint's env and prod.
Don't: skip nodeSelector. A toleration only allows; it does not send.

Vim tip: type :set paste before you press i and paste. Save with :wq.

questions.title: Rolling update and rollback

pic.say: Roll out a new version, then roll back.

questions.words:
• Rolling update = new pods replace old ones a few at a time. The app stays up.
  • Revision = each change of the pod template gets a new number. Old ones are kept.
questions.think:
• Wanted: update, roll back, then the image in a file.
  • Look first: the container name and the current image.
  • Expect: container nginx, image nginx:1.27.
  • Fix: set image, rollout status, rollout undo, jsonpath into the file.
  • Prove: the file says nginx:1.27.
questions.setup:
k delete namespace shop --ignore-not-found
rm -f /root/image.txt
k create namespace shop
k create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=3 -n shop
k rollout status deployment/web --timeout=120s -n shop
clear
k get deployment web -o wide -n shop
questions.question:
In namespace `shop`:
1. Update deployment `web` to image `nginx:1.28` and wait until the rollout is complete.
2. Then roll the deployment back to the previous revision.
3. Write the image that is in use after the rollback to `/root/image.txt`.
questions.meaning: Change the image, wait, undo, then save the current image to a file.

steps.title: Step 1. What is the container called?
steps.html:
Why: set image needs the container name, not the deployment name.

k get deployment web -o wide -n shop

You see:

NAME   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE   CONTAINERS   IMAGES       SELECTOR
web    3/3     3            3           1m    nginx        nginx:1.27   app=web   <-- nginx

Means: the container is nginx. The old image is nginx:1.27.

flow.h: Why: set image needs the container name, not the deployment name.

flow.t: k get deployment web -o wide -n shop

flow.h: You see:

flow.t:
NAME   READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE   CONTAINERS   IMAGES       SELECTOR
web    3/3     3            3           1m    nginx        nginx:1.27   app=web   <-- nginx

flow.h: Means: the container is nginx. The old image is nginx:1.27.

steps.title: Step 2. Update the image and wait
steps.html:
Why: rollout status waits until all new pods are ready.

k set image deployment/web nginx=nginx:1.28 -n shop
k rollout status deployment/web -n shop

You see:

deployment.apps/web image updated
Waiting for deployment "web" rollout to finish: 1 out of 3 new replicas have been updated...
...
deployment "web" successfully rolled out

Don't: write web=nginx:1.28. Left of = is the container name.

flow.h: Why: rollout status waits until all new pods are ready.

flow.t: k set image deployment/web nginx=nginx:1.28 -n shop

flow.h: You see:

flow.t:
deployment.apps/web image updated
Waiting for deployment "web" rollout to finish: 1 out of 3 new replicas have been updated...
...
deployment "web" successfully rolled out

flow.h: Don't: write web=nginx:1.28. Left of = is the container name.

steps.title: Step 3. Roll back
steps.html:
Why: undo goes back to the previous revision.

k rollout history deployment/web -n shop
k rollout undo deployment/web -n shop
k rollout status deployment/web -n shop

You see:

REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
1         <none>
2         <none>  <-- 1.28
deployment.apps/web rolled back
deployment "web" successfully rolled out

Don't: run undo twice. The second one goes back to nginx:1.28.

flow.h: Why: undo goes back to the previous revision.
You see:

flow.t:
REVISION  CHANGE-CAUSE
1         <none>
2         <none>  <-- 1.28

questions.title: PV + PVC + Pod (build the whole chain)

pic.say: Build the disk chain: PV → PVC → Pod.

questions.words:
• PV = PersistentVolume, a disk for the whole cluster. No namespace.
  • PVC = PersistentVolumeClaim, a request for a disk. It lives in a namespace.
  • storageClassName = a group name. PV and PVC must have the same one to connect.
questions.think:
• Wanted: a pod that uses a claim that uses a disk.
  • Look first: one docs page has all three files.
  • Expect: the PVC shows Bound to pv-data.
  • Fix: build right to left: PV, then PVC, then pod.
  • Prove: pod Running; the PV is Bound to storage/pvc-data.
questions.setup:
k delete namespace storage --ignore-not-found
k delete pv pv-data --ignore-not-found
rm -f pv.yaml pvc.yaml pod.yaml
k create namespace storage
clear
k get pv,pvc -n storage
questions.question:
1. Create a PersistentVolume named `pv-data`: capacity `1Gi`, access mode `ReadWriteOnce`, hostPath `/mnt/data`, storage class `manual`.
2. In namespace `storage`, create a PersistentVolumeClaim named `pvc-data` that requests `500Mi`, access mode `ReadWriteOnce`, storage class `manual`.
3. In namespace `storage`, create a pod named `web-store` with image `nginx:1.27` that mounts the claim at `/usr/share/nginx/html`.
questions.meaning: Build the chain Pod → PVC → PV, starting with the disk.

steps.title: Step 1. Make the disk (PV)
steps.html:
Why: there is no k create pv. Copy pv-volume.yaml from the docs page "Configure a Pod to Use a PersistentVolume for Storage".

vim pv.yaml

The finished file. Only name: pv-data and storage: 1Gi differ from the docs:

apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: pv-data
spec:
  storageClassName: manual
  capacity:
    storage: 1Gi
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  hostPath:
    path: "/mnt/data"
k apply -f pv.yaml
k get pv

You see:

NAME      CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS      CLAIM   STORAGECLASS   ...
pv-data   1Gi        RWO            Retain           Available           manual         ...   <-- free

Means: the disk exists. Also delete the docs' labels: and type: local lines.
Don't: add namespace:. A PV belongs to the whole cluster.

Vim tip: type :set paste before you press i and paste. Save with :wq.

flow.h: Why: there is no k create pv. Copy pv-volume.yaml from the docs page "Configure a Pod to Use a PersistentVolume for Storage".

steps.title: Step 2. Ask for the disk (PVC)
steps.html:
Why: a pod cannot use a PV directly. Copy pv-claim.yaml from the same page.

vim pvc.yaml

The finished file. Only name:, namespace: and storage: 500Mi differ from the docs:

apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: pvc-data
  namespace: storage
spec:
  storageClassName: manual
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 500Mi
k apply -f pvc.yaml
k get pvc -n storage

You see:

NAME       STATUS   VOLUME    CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS   ...
pvc-data   Bound    pv-data   1Gi        RWO            manual         ...   <-- Bound

Means: class and mode match, and 1Gi fits 500Mi. CAPACITY 1Gi is correct: the claim gets the whole disk.
Don't: go on before you see Bound.

steps.html:
Why: copy pv-pod.yaml from the same page.

vim pod.yaml

The finished file. Only name:, namespace:, claimName: and image: differ from the docs:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web-store
  namespace: storage
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: task-pv-storage
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: pvc-data
  containers:
    - name: task-pv-container
      image: nginx:1.27
      ports:
        - containerPort: 80
          name: "http-server"
      volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: "/usr/share/nginx/html"
          name: task-pv-storage
k apply -f pod.yaml

You see:

pod/web-store created

Means: claimName is the PVC's name. task-pv-storage only links volumes to volumeMounts.
Don't: rename task-pv-storage in one place only. Both must match.

questions.title: Reuse an existing PV (the MariaDB question)

pic.say: Reconnect an app to its old disk without losing data.

questions.words:
• PV = PersistentVolume, a disk for the whole cluster. Here it holds the database.
  • PVC = PersistentVolumeClaim, a request for a disk. A pod uses a PVC, never a PV.
questions.think:
• Wanted: Pod → new PVC → the OLD PV.
  • Look first: the PV's size, access mode and class.
  • Expect: Available, 250Mi, RWO, empty class.
  • Fix: a PVC with the same three values; claimName: mariadb in the file.
  • Prove: pod Running; the PV is Bound to mariadb/mariadb.
questions.setup:
k delete namespace mariadb --ignore-not-found
k delete pv mariadb-pv --ignore-not-found
rm -f pvc.yaml
k create namespace mariadb
cat <<EOF | k apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata:
  name: mariadb-pv
spec:
  capacity:
    storage: 250Mi
  accessModes:
  - ReadWriteOnce
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: ""
  hostPath:
    path: /mnt/mariadb
EOF
cat > /root/mariadb-deploy.yaml <<EOF
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: mariadb
  namespace: mariadb
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: mariadb
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: mariadb
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: mariadb
        image: mariadb:11
        env:
        - name: MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD
          value: secret
        volumeMounts:
        - name: data
          mountPath: /var/lib/mysql
      volumes:
      - name: data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: ""
EOF
clear
k get pv mariadb-pv
questions.question:
A MariaDB deployment in namespace `mariadb` was deleted by accident. Its PersistentVolume still exists and holds the data.
1. Create a PersistentVolumeClaim named `mariadb` in namespace `mariadb`, with access mode `ReadWriteOnce` and `250Mi` of storage. It must bind to the existing PersistentVolume.
2. Edit `/root/mariadb-deploy.yaml` so the deployment uses this PVC.
3. Apply the file and make sure the deployment is running.
questions.meaning: Write a PVC that matches the old disk, then point the app at it.

steps.title: Step 1. Read the old disk
steps.html:
Why: a PVC never names the disk. It binds to a PV with the same class, mode and enough size.

You see:

NAME         CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS      CLAIM   STORAGECLASS   ...
mariadb-pv   250Mi      RWO            Retain           Available                          ...   <-- no class

Means: 250Mi, ReadWriteOnce, free, and no class. Your PVC must repeat these.

You see:

flow.t:

mariadb-pv   250Mi      RWO            Retain           Available                          ...   <-- no class

steps.title: Step 2. Write the PVC and bind it
steps.html:
Why: there is no k create pvc. Copy pv-claim.yaml from the docs page "Configure a Pod to Use a PersistentVolume for Storage".

questions.question:
ssh cka01001

world.goal:
📝 Bring node01 (Team Alpha) back to Ready.
Fix must survive a reboot.

scenes.say: Welcome to your software company. Upstairs is the leadership room: the control plane. Jira, the API server, takes every request and checks permissions. Jira's database, etcd, holds the truth. The work assigner, the scheduler, gives each new work item to a team with capacity. And the Release Train Engineer, the controller manager, keeps reality matching the plan.

Downstairs is Team Alpha's room: node zero one. The team lead, the container runtime, gets the developers working. And the Scrum Master, the kubelet, takes the assigned work, and at every sync reports to Jira: team healthy!
scenes.sub: kubelet = Scrum Master → reports "team healthy" at every sync

scenes.say: But today, the Scrum Master doesn't show up. No sync, no report. After forty seconds, the Release Train Engineer marks Team Alpha as not reporting: node zero one, Not Ready. And the work assigner stops giving the team new work.
scenes.sub: No report for 40 s → node01 NotReady → no new work

scenes.say: Your exam task: bring node zero one back to Ready. And the fix must survive a reboot. Remember that last part.
Quick question. Why is node zero one Not Ready?

quiz.t: 🧑‍🔧 The Team Lead (container runtime) is off sick
quiz.fb: Not quite. Without the team lead the work would stall, but the Scrum Master would still report. Nobody is reporting at all.

quiz.t: 🧑‍💼 The Scrum Master (kubelet) isn't doing the job
quiz.fb: Exactly! No Scrum Master, no team healthy report, so the team is marked Not Ready.
Not quite. If Jira were down, nobody could see anything, not even k get nodes.

scenes.say: So go to the team's room. S S H node zero one. Your terminal now works inside Team Alpha's room. Look at the prompt: it says node zero one.
scenes.sub: ssh node01 = walk into Team Alpha's room

scenes.say: Every role in the room has an official assignment. That's system control. System control status kubelet asks: is the Scrum Master doing the job? Answer: inactive, dead. Nobody is.
scenes.sub: systemctl = role assignment · status = is anyone doing the job?

scenes.roster: kubelet · active (running) · covering this sprint only
scenes.say: Easy fix: system control start kubelet. Someone covers the role for this sprint. The Scrum Master reports again, Team Alpha is Ready. Done? Not so fast.
scenes.sub: systemctl start = cover the role… this sprint only

scenes.say: Twist! Next week there's a reorg. That's a reboot. And Team Alpha has no Scrum Master again! Why? Start only covered the role for one sprint. Nobody was officially assigned.
scenes.sub: TWIST: reorg (reboot) → no Scrum Master again

scenes.say: So which command officially assigns the Scrum Master, and starts the job right now?

quiz.fb: That's the trap we just fell into. Start only covers this sprint.
Yes! Enable makes the assignment official, so it survives every reorg. Dash dash now also starts it right away.
That command doesn't exist. And kubectl only talks to Jira, not to the role assignments in the team room.

scenes.say: System control enable, dash dash now, kubelet. Enable: officially assigned, so the role survives every reorg. Dash dash now: start right now.
scenes.sub: enable = official, survives reboots · --now = right now

scenes.say: Another reorg. And this time? The Scrum Master is still there. The fix survives a reboot.
scenes.sub: Reorg again → Scrum Master still there ✓

scenes.say: Go back to the leadership room with exit, and check Jira with k get nodes. Node zero one: Ready. Task done!
scenes.sub: exit = back to leadership · k get nodes = check Jira

scenes.say: Remember: Not Ready means the Scrum Master, the kubelet, isn't doing the job. Go to the team with S S H. Check with status. And never just start it: enable dash dash now, so it survives the reorg.
scenes.sub: NotReady → ssh → status → enable --now → exit → get nodes

questions.title: CrashLoop / restarts: wrong liveness probe
questions.question:
ssh cka01004
Deployment api in namespace web keeps restarting its Pods. Identify the cause and fix it. The nginx container listens on port 80. Do not delete the Deployment.
questions.setup:
kubectl create namespace web --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: api, namespace: web}
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: api}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.27-alpine
        ports: [{containerPort: 80}]
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet: {path: /, port: 8080}
          initialDelaySeconds: 3
          periodSeconds: 3
          failureThreshold: 2
EOF
questions.meaning: The health check knocks on the wrong door (8080) so Kubernetes keeps restarting the pod.
questions.words: • livenessProbe = a URL the kubelet calls again and again (N failures in a row = container restarted)

flow.t:
NAME      READY   STATUS    RESTARTS     AGE
api-...   1/1     Running   3 (5s ago)   40s   <-- RESTARTS grows (or CrashLoopBackOff)

flow.h: Growing RESTARTS = something kills the container.

flow.t: k describe pods -l app=api -n web | grep -i -A2 liveness

Liveness:     http-get http://:8080/ delay=3s timeout=1s period=3s #success=1 #failure=2   <-- 8080
...
  Warning  Unhealthy  ...  kubelet  Liveness probe failed: Get "http://...:8080/": dial tcp ...:8080: connect: connection refused

flow.h: Probe checks port 8080 but nginx uses 80. Shortened: ... marks parts of the real output left out.
In vim change the probe port 8080 to 80. Esc, :wq, Enter → deployment.apps/api edited. Probe now checks the port nginx really uses. Edit the Deployment, not the Pod.

flow.t:
deployment "api" successfully rolled out
NAME      READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
api-...   1/1     Running   0          30s   <-- new pod, RESTARTS 0

flow.h: The NEW pod (new name) shows RESTARTS 0 and stays healthy; the old one disappears.

questions.title: Install cri-dockerd + kernel sysctl
questions.question:
ssh cka01007
Prepare this node for a Docker-based container runtime:
- Install the Debian package /root/cri-dockerd.deb using dpkg.
- Enable and start the cri-docker service.
- Configure these kernel parameters so they persist across reboots (file /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf):
  net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables = 1
  net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
  net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 1
  net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 131072
questions.setup:
test -f /root/cri-dockerd.deb || curl -fsSLo /root/cri-dockerd.deb https://github.com/Mirantis/cri-dockerd/releases/download/v0.3.16/cri-dockerd_0.3.16.3-0.ubuntu-jammy_amd64.deb || echo "download failed - check release page"
ls -l /root/cri-dockerd.deb || echo "MISSING: download a cri-dockerd .deb for your Ubuntu from https://github.com/Mirantis/cri-dockerd/releases to /root/cri-dockerd.deb"
questions.meaning: Install a runtime package and turn on 4 Linux network settings permanently. On Killercoda Docker is absent, so cri-docker will not start. The jammy .deb may not match a newer Ubuntu. dpkg, enable and sysctl still practise.
questions.words:
• sysctl = a Linux kernel setting
  • kernel module = a driver loaded with modprobe, needed before some sysctl settings exist

flow.h: dpkg, systemctl and /etc need root. The real exam requires sudo -i. Killercoda is already root. If the file is missing on Killercoda, the setup download failed. Download a .deb from the cri-dockerd releases page. Or just practise the commands.

dpkg installs a local .deb file. If dpkg stops with missing dependencies, run apt-get -f install -y. Then check again. Status iU means unpacked but not configured yet. ii means installed. Shortened: ... marks parts of the real output left out.

flow.t:
Job for cri-docker.service failed because the control process exited with error code.
...
enabled

flow.h: enable = at boot, --now = start now. Killercoda has no Docker, so the start fails there (first line), but the enable still worked: is-enabled says enabled. In the exam (Docker present) there is no error. Shortened: ... marks parts of the real output left out.

flow.t:
cat <<'EOF' > /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables = 1
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 1
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 131072
EOF

flow.h: Files in /etc/sysctl.d survive reboots. Paste the whole block at once, including the final EOF line. Everything between the two EOFs goes into the file.

steps.title: Load the kernel modules now and at every boot

flow.h: bridge-nf-call-iptables only exists when br_netfilter is loaded, nf_conntrack_max needs nf_conntrack. modprobe loads them now. The modules-load.d file loads them after a reboot. So the sysctl settings really persist.
Applies all /etc/sysctl.d files without rebooting.

questions.mug:
sudo -i
ls -l /root/cri-dockerd.deb
dpkg -i /root/cri-dockerd.deb
systemctl enable --now cri-docker.service
systemctl is-enabled cri-docker
cat <<'EOF' > /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables = 1
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1
net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 1
net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max = 131072
EOF
modprobe br_netfilter
modprobe nf_conntrack
printf 'br_netfilter\nnf_conntrack\n' > /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf
sysctl --system | grep -E "bridge-nf-call-iptables|ip_forward|all.forwarding|conntrack_max"
dpkg -l | grep cri-dockerd
systemctl is-enabled cri-docker
sysctl net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables net.ipv4.ip_forward net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max
cat /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf
questions.docs: kubernetes.io: Container Runtimes (search: cri-dockerd, sysctl ip_forward)

questions.question:
ssh cka01011
Migrate the existing Ingress web in namespace web-app to the Gateway API, keeping HTTPS:
- Create a Gateway named web-gateway using GatewayClass nginx, with an HTTPS listener on port 443 for hostname gateway.web.example. Use the TLS Secret web-tls already referenced by the Ingress.

kubectl create namespace web-app --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
openssl req -x509 -nodes -newkey rsa:2048 -days 365 -subj "/CN=gateway.web.example" -keyout /tmp/web-tls.key -out /tmp/web-tls.crt 2>/dev/null
kubectl create secret tls web-tls --cert=/tmp/web-tls.crt --key=/tmp/web-tls.key --dry-run=client -o yaml -n web-app | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata: {name: nginx}
spec: {controllerName: example.net/gateway-controller}
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: web, namespace: web-app}
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: web}}
    spec:
      containers: [{name: nginx, image: nginx:1.27-alpine, ports: [{containerPort: 80}]}]
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: {name: web, namespace: web-app}
spec: {selector: {app: web}, ports: [{port: 80, targetPort: 80}]}
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata: {name: web, namespace: web-app}
spec:
  tls: [{hosts: [gateway.web.example], secretName: web-tls}]
  rules:
  - host: gateway.web.example
    http:
      paths:
      - {path: /, pathType: Prefix, backend: {service: {name: web, port: {number: 80}}}}
EOF
questions.meaning: Rebuild the HTTPS Ingress as a Gateway (door + certificate). Add an HTTPRoute (path to service). No Gateway controller runs on Killercoda, so status stays Unknown - that is fine.

• GatewayClass = which controller runs the Gateway
  • listener = port + protocol + hostname (+ TLS certificate)
  • parentRefs = the Gateway it attaches to

flow.h: Gateway must use an existing class.

flow.t:
cat <<'EOF' > gw.yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata: {name: web-gateway, namespace: web-app}
spec:
  gatewayClassName: nginx
  listeners:
  - name: https
    protocol: HTTPS
    port: 443
    hostname: gateway.web.example
    tls:
      mode: Terminate
      certificateRefs:
      - {kind: Secret, name: web-tls}
EOF

flow.h: Gateway = the entry door with TLS. Ingress host -> listener hostname. Ingress tls.secretName -> certificateRefs. Terminate = the Gateway decrypts HTTPS with that Secret.

flow.t:

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata: {name: web-route, namespace: web-app}
spec:
  parentRefs: [{name: web-gateway}]
  hostnames: [gateway.web.example]
  rules:
  - matches: [{path: {type: PathPrefix, value: /}}]
    backendRefs: [{name: web, port: 80}]
EOF

flow.h: Route = which traffic goes to which Service (Ingress paths/backend -> rules/backendRefs). parentRefs needs no namespace because the route is in the same namespace as the Gateway.

questions.title: NetworkPolicy: choose the least permissive
questions.question:
ssh cka01012
Pods of Deployment frontend (namespace frontend) must be able to reach Pods of Deployment backend (namespace backend) on port 80. A deny-all policy already exists in namespace backend.
Review the NetworkPolicy files in /root/netpol/ and apply the ONE that allows this traffic with the least permissions. Do not delete or modify the existing policies.
questions.meaning: Pick the rule file that opens only the needed door, nothing more.
questions.words:
• NetworkPolicy = a firewall rule for pods
  • default-deny = blocks all incoming traffic to the namespace's pods
  • ingress from = who may connect, picked by namespace label and/or pod label

flow.t: k exec deployment/frontend -n frontend -- wget -qO- -T2 backend.backend

wget: download timed out
command terminated with exit code 1

flow.h: Deny-all is in effect. backend.backend = <service>.<namespace>. If this already works, your playground's network plugin ignores NetworkPolicies. Continue anyway. The choice of file is what is graded.

Key rule: in ONE "- from" item, namespaceSelector and podSelector must BOTH match (AND). As separate items, either one is enough (OR). 1 opens everything to all pods. 3 opens all namespaces on all ports. 2 = only frontend pods from namespace frontend, only TCP 80.
Only frontend pods, only port 80.

questions.title: HPA with scale-down behavior
questions.question:
ssh cka01014
Create a HorizontalPodAutoscaler named apache-server in namespace autoscale for the existing Deployment apache-server. It must target 50% CPU utilisation per Pod, with a minimum of 1 and a maximum of 4 replicas. Set the scale-down stabilization window to 30 seconds.
questions.meaning: Auto-add pods when CPU > 50%, and wait 30 s before removing them.
questions.words:
• HPA (HorizontalPodAutoscaler) = changes a Deployment's replica count based on load
  • metrics-server = the add-on that measures pod CPU for it
  • stabilization window = how long the HPA waits before scaling down

flow.t:
cat <<'EOF' > hpa.yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: {name: apache-server, namespace: autoscale}
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: {apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: apache-server}
  minReplicas: 1
  maxReplicas: 4
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource: {name: cpu, target: {type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 50}}
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 30
EOF

flow.h: behavior only exists in autoscaling/v2 YAML. behavior sits directly under spec, scaleDown under behavior.

flow.t:
NAME            REFERENCE                  TARGETS              MINPODS   MAXPODS   REPLICAS   AGE
apache-server   Deployment/apache-server   cpu: <unknown>/50%   1         4         1          20s

flow.h: <unknown> = no metrics-server is installed in the playground. So there are no CPU numbers yet. The HPA object itself is still correct.

flow.t: k get hpa apache-server -o jsonpath="{.spec.behavior.scaleDown}" -n autoscale

flow.h: Proves behavior was saved. Kubernetes adds the default policies and selectPolicy itself; only the 30 matters.

questions.title: Default StorageClass with WaitForFirstConsumer
questions.question:
ssh cka01015
Create a StorageClass named local-fast with provisioner rancher.io/local-path and volume binding mode WaitForFirstConsumer. Make it the default StorageClass; it must be the ONLY default. Do not modify existing PersistentVolumeClaims.
questions.setup:
kubectl get deployments -A | grep -q local-path-provisioner || kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rancher/local-path-provisioner/v0.0.30/deploy/local-path-storage.yaml
kubectl patch storageclass local-path -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class":"true"}}}'
questions.meaning: Add a storage type and make it the only automatic choice.
questions.words:
• StorageClass = a type of disk Kubernetes can create on demand
  • default class = the one used by a PVC that names no class
  • WaitForFirstConsumer = create the disk only when a pod that uses it is scheduled

flow.t:
NAME                   PROVISIONER             RECLAIMPOLICY   VOLUMEBINDINGMODE      ALLOWVOLUMEEXPANSION   AGE
local-path (default)   rancher.io/local-path   Delete          WaitForFirstConsumer   false                  ...

flow.h: "(default)" marks the current default. Note EVERY class marked (default).
Remove the old default before adding the new one, so there are never two defaults. Repeat this command for each other class marked (default) in step 1. Change only the name.

flow.t:
cat <<'EOF' | k apply -f -
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: local-fast
  annotations: {storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class: "true"}
provisioner: rancher.io/local-path
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
EOF

flow.h: The annotation (value "true" in quotes) makes it the default.

flow.t:

questions.title: Reuse a retained PV for MariaDB
questions.question:
ssh cka01016
A MariaDB Deployment in namespace mariadb was deleted by mistake, but its PersistentVolume mariadb-pv was kept.
- Create a PersistentVolumeClaim named mariadb in namespace mariadb: access mode ReadWriteOnce, storage 250Mi, so that it binds to the existing PV.
- Edit /root/mariadb-deploy.yaml so the Deployment uses this PVC, then apply it. Ensure the Pod is Running.
questions.setup:
kubectl create namespace mariadb --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
cat <<'EOF' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolume
metadata: {name: mariadb-pv}
spec:
  capacity: {storage: 250Mi}
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy: Retain
  storageClassName: ""
  hostPath: {path: /mnt/data/mariadb, type: DirectoryOrCreate}
EOF
cat <<'EOF' > /root/mariadb-deploy.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: {name: mariadb, namespace: mariadb}
spec:
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: mariadb}}
  template:
    metadata: {labels: {app: mariadb}}
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: mariadb
        image: mariadb:11
        env: [{name: MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD, value: cka}]
        volumeMounts: [{name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/mysql}]
      volumes:
      - name: data
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: ""
EOF
questions.meaning: Make a storage claim that grabs the old disk. Then plug it into the database deployment.
questions.words:
• PV (PersistentVolume) = the disk
  • PVC (PersistentVolumeClaim) = a request for a disk
  • Bound = request matched to a disk
  • RWO (ReadWriteOnce) = one node can mount it read-write

flow.t:
NAME         CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   RECLAIM POLICY   STATUS      CLAIM   STORAGECLASS   ...
mariadb-pv   250Mi      RWO            Retain           Available                          ...

flow.h: Note size, mode and empty class. If STATUS is Released (common in the exam), the PV still remembers its old claim. Run k patch pv mariadb-pv -p '{"spec":{"claimRef":null}}'. Then it becomes Available. Shortened: ... marks parts of the real output left out.

flow.t:
cat <<'EOF' | k apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: {name: mariadb, namespace: mariadb}
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: ""
  volumeName: mariadb-pv
  resources: {requests: {storage: 250Mi}}
EOF

flow.h: Empty class "" stops the default class grabbing it. volumeName: mariadb-pv guarantees it binds to exactly that PV.

flow.t:
NAME      STATUS   VOLUME       CAPACITY   ACCESS MODES   STORAGECLASS   ...
mariadb   Bound    mariadb-pv   250Mi      RWO                           ...

flow.h: Bound to the old PV = old data kept. Shortened: ... marks parts of the real output left out.

steps.title: Point the Deployment to the PVC

flow.h: sed -i 's/OLD/NEW/' file = replace text inside the file. Here claimName: "" becomes claimName: mariadb. grep shows the result before you apply.

flow.t:
NAME          READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
mariadb-...   1/1     Running   0          40s

flow.h: Database runs on the kept disk.

questions.title: Kubelet fails: broken systemd drop-in
questions.question:
ssh cka02001
Node node01 is NotReady after a maintenance change. Find out why the kubelet does not start on node01 and fix it. Do not reinstall any packages.
questions.setup:
ssh node01 "sed -i 's#/usr/bin/kubelet #/usr/local/bin/kubelet #' /usr/lib/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf 2>/dev/null; systemctl daemon-reload; systemctl restart kubelet"
sleep 60
questions.meaning: The kubelet service file points to a program path that does not exist; correct it.
questions.words:
• unit file = systemd's recipe for starting a service
  • drop-in = an extra file in kubelet.service.d/ that overrides parts of the main unit

flow.t:
NAME           STATUS     ROLES           AGE   VERSION
controlplane   Ready      control-plane   ...   ...
node01         NotReady   <none>          ...   ...

flow.h: Start from the symptom. If it still says Ready, wait 30 s and run it again. The grace period is ~50 s.

steps.title: Log in, become root and check kubelet

flow.t:
...
     Active: activating (auto-restart) (Result: exit-code) since ...
    Process: ... ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/kubelet $KUBELET_KUBECONFIG_ARGS ... (code=exited, status=203/EXEC)
...

flow.h: 203/EXEC = binary path not found. sudo -i = become root (exam only; Killercoda is already root). Shortened: ... marks parts of the real output left out.

flow.t:
... kubelet.service: Failed to locate executable /usr/local/bin/kubelet: No such file or directory
... kubelet.service: Failed at step EXEC spawning /usr/local/bin/kubelet: No such file or directory
... kubelet.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=203/EXEC
...

flow.h: Logs show the wrong path. Shortened: ... marks parts of the real output left out.

steps.title: Find the real binary and the config

flow.t:
/usr/bin/kubelet  <-- which
ExecStart=/usr/bin/kubelet
ExecStart=  <-- clears it
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/kubelet $KUBELET_KUBECONFIG_ARGS ...

flow.h: Line 2 comes from the main unit, lines 3 and 4 from the drop-in. The LAST ExecStart wins - it points to /usr/local/bin/kubelet, which does not exist. The real binary is /usr/bin/kubelet.
Each "# /path" line is a file systemd reads. Note the 10-kubeadm.conf path (it may be under /etc/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/ instead).

In vim (path from the previous step): on the ExecStart= line change /usr/local/bin/kubelet to /usr/bin/kubelet; Esc :wq. daemon-reload makes systemd re-read the changed file; restart starts kubelet with the right path. Two exits: leave root, leave node01.

flow.t:
NAME           STATUS   ROLES           AGE   VERSION
controlplane   Ready    control-plane   ...   ...
node01         Ready    <none>          ...   ...

flow.h: Allow ~30s.

questions.mug:
k get nodes
ssh node01
sudo -i
systemctl status kubelet --no-pager | head -12
journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager | tail -5
which kubelet
systemctl cat kubelet | grep ExecStart=
systemctl cat kubelet | grep '^# /'
vim /usr/lib/systemd/system/kubelet.service.d/10-kubeadm.conf
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl restart kubelet
systemctl is-active kubelet
exit
exit
k get nodes
k get nodes
ssh node01 systemctl is-active kubelet

story.broken: The cook's (kubelet's) job sheet (systemd drop-in) points to a program path that doesn't exist.
story.fix: Fix the path in the drop-in, systemctl daemon-reload, restart kubelet.

coach.pattern: Node NotReady → kubelet fails → fix systemd drop-in path

clues.means: Someone edited config: check systemctl cat kubelet

clues.q: why the kubelet does not start on node01
clues.means: ssh node01; systemctl status + journalctl -u kubelet
Fix the unit/drop-in file, not apt

traps.do: `systemctl daemon-reload; systemctl restart kubelet`, because systemd rereads unit files only after daemon-reload

`ssh node01; sudo -i` first, because system files need root, else Permission denied

questions.title: Scheduler down: Pods stay Pending
questions.question:
ssh cka02002
A new Pod named stuck in namespace default stays Pending, even though nodes have free resources. Diagnose and repair the cluster component responsible so that the Pod is scheduled.
keys: fix the control plane component, not the pod
questions.setup:
sed -i 's#^    - kube-scheduler$#    - kube-schedulerr#' /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
sleep 20
kubectl run stuck --image=nginx:1.27-alpine --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
questions.meaning: The scheduler program is broken by a typo in its file. Fix the file, not the pod.
questions.words:
• scheduler = the control-plane part that picks a node for each new pod
  • static pod = a pod the kubelet runs from a YAML file in /etc/kubernetes/manifests
  • mirror pod = the read-only copy of it you see in kubectl

steps.title: See the pod has no node

flow.t:
NAME    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   IP       NODE     NOMINATED NODE   READINESS GATES
stuck   0/1     Pending   0          1m    <none>   <none>   <none>           <none>

flow.h: No events at all = nobody is scheduling.

flow.t: k get pods -n kube-system | grep scheduler

flow.h: Scheduler is a static pod on controlplane. STATUS alternates between RunContainerError and CrashLoopBackOff.

steps.title: Read why the container cannot start

flow.t: k describe pods -l component=kube-scheduler -n kube-system | grep -iE 'reason|message'

Reason:       CrashLoopBackOff
      Reason:       StartError
      Message:      ... exec: "kube-schedulerr": executable file not found in $PATH: unknown

flow.h: Typo in the command. Reason may also read RunContainerError. crictl logs shows NOTHING here: the program never started, so it printed no log. The error is in the pod status (describe). Or check journalctl -u kubelet | grep scheduler. Shortened: ... marks parts of the real output left out.

steps.title: Become root and fix the static pod manifest

flow.h: Files in /etc/kubernetes/manifests need root (exam: sudo -i; Killercoda is already root). sed -i 's#OLD#NEW#' replaces text in the file. kubelet notices the change and recreates the scheduler pod by itself (~30 s).

kube-scheduler-controlplane            1/1     Running   0          40s
NAME    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE   IP     NODE     ...
stuck   1/1     Running   0          5m    ...    node01   ...

questions.question:
ssh cka02003
Pods can no longer resolve Service names. Fix cluster DNS so that, from Pod dns-test in namespace lookup, the name kubernetes.default resolves. Save the output of that nslookup to /root/dns.txt.

kubectl create namespace lookup --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
kubectl run dns-test --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never --dry-run=client -o yaml -n lookup -- sleep 36000 | kubectl apply -f -

  • CoreDNS = the coredns Deployment pods in kube-system that answer in-cluster name lookups
